topics.label: Meaningful Naming
topics.desc: Choosing intention-revealing, pronounceable, searchable names for variables, functions, and types so code reads like prose and reviewers infer purpose without comments.

topics.label: Small Functions
topics.desc: Keeping functions short and doing one thing at a single level of abstraction, so they fit in your head, are easy to name, test, and reuse.

topics.label: Readability
topics.desc: Optimizing code for the human reader since it is read far more than written, favoring clear control flow, consistent formatting, and low cognitive load over cleverness.

topics.label: Self-Documenting Code
topics.desc: Expressing intent through clear names and structure so the code explains itself, reserving comments for the why and tricky context rather than restating the what.

topics.label: Comments & Documentation
topics.desc: Writing comments that add value, the rationale, caveats, and TODOs, while avoiding redundant or stale comments and using doc formats like JSDoc, docstrings, or TSDoc.

topics.label: Code Smells
topics.desc: Surface symptoms hinting at deeper problems, such as long methods, large classes, duplicated code, long parameter lists, and feature envy, that signal a refactor.

topics.label: Guard Clauses
topics.desc: Returning early on invalid or edge inputs at the top of a function to flatten nesting and avoid deep if-else pyramids, keeping the happy path linear.

topics.label: Boy-Scout Rule
topics.desc: Leaving code a little cleaner than you found it on every change, so quality improves incrementally through many small touch-ups rather than rare big rewrites.

topics.label: Avoiding Premature Abstraction
topics.desc: Resisting speculative generality and the wrong abstraction; inline duplication is often cheaper than a leaky shared abstraction until the real pattern is clear.

topics.label: Single Responsibility
topics.desc: The S in SOLID: a module or class should have one reason to change, owning a single responsibility so unrelated concerns do not force entangled edits.

topics.label: Open-Closed Principle
topics.desc: The O in SOLID: software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification, adding behavior via new code rather than editing tested existing code.

topics.label: Liskov Substitution
topics.desc: The L in SOLID: subtypes must be usable anywhere their base type is expected without breaking correctness, honoring the contract of what they replace.

topics.label: Interface Segregation
topics.desc: The I in SOLID: prefer many small, focused interfaces over one fat interface, so clients depend only on the methods they actually use.

topics.label: Dependency Inversion
topics.desc: The D in SOLID: high-level modules and details should both depend on abstractions, not concretions, inverting source dependencies toward stable interfaces.

topics.label: DRY
topics.desc: Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge should have a single authoritative representation, removing duplication of logic so one change propagates everywhere.

topics.label: KISS
topics.desc: Keep It Simple: favor the simplest design that solves the problem, since unnecessary complexity costs comprehension, bugs, and future change far more than it saves.

topics.label: YAGNI
topics.desc: You Aren't Gonna Need It: build only what current requirements demand, deferring speculative features and flexibility until a concrete need actually appears.

topics.label: Separation of Concerns
topics.desc: Splitting a system into distinct parts that each address one concern, like UI, business logic, and persistence, so they evolve and reason independently.

topics.label: Coupling & Cohesion
topics.desc: The twin metrics of good design: aim for low coupling between modules and high cohesion within them, so components are independent yet internally focused.

topics.label: Composition Over Inheritance
topics.desc: Preferring to assemble behavior from small collaborating objects rather than deep inheritance hierarchies, gaining flexibility and avoiding fragile base-class coupling.

topics.label: Law of Demeter
topics.desc: The principle of least knowledge: an object should only talk to its immediate collaborators, not reach through chains of getters, reducing structural coupling.

topics.label: Single Source of Truth
topics.desc: Storing each fact or piece of state in exactly one canonical place that everything else derives from, preventing inconsistency between duplicated copies of data.

topics.label: MVC & MVVM
topics.desc: Presentation patterns separating data (model), display (view), and coordination (controller or view-model with data binding), the backbone of most web frameworks.

topics.label: Repository Pattern
topics.desc: An abstraction that mediates between domain logic and data storage, exposing collection-like methods so business code is decoupled from ORM or query details.

topics.label: Factory Pattern
topics.desc: A creational pattern that centralizes object creation behind a method or class, choosing the concrete type to build so callers depend on an interface, not a constructor.

topics.label: Singleton
topics.desc: A pattern ensuring a class has one shared instance with a global access point, common for config or connection pools but often criticized as hidden global state.

topics.label: Observer & Pub-Sub
topics.desc: A behavioral pattern where subjects notify subscribers of changes, decoupling producers from consumers; the basis of event emitters, signals, and message buses.

topics.label: Strategy Pattern
topics.desc: Encapsulating interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface so behavior can be selected or swapped at runtime, often replacing sprawling conditional branches.

topics.label: Adapter Pattern
topics.desc: A structural pattern that wraps an incompatible interface in one a client expects, letting otherwise mismatched classes or third-party libraries work together.

topics.label: Decorator Pattern
topics.desc: Wrapping an object to add behavior dynamically without changing its class, composing layers of functionality; seen in middleware, HOCs, and stream wrappers.

topics.label: Dependency Injection & IoC
topics.desc: Supplying a component's collaborators from outside rather than constructing them internally, inverting control via constructors or containers for testable, decoupled code.

topics.label: Module Pattern
topics.desc: Encapsulating related code with a clear public interface while hiding internals, historically via closures and IIFEs, now largely via native ES modules.

topics.label: Folder & File Organization
topics.desc: Conventions for naming and grouping files and directories so a codebase is navigable and predictable, letting any contributor guess where code lives.

topics.label: Layered Architecture
topics.desc: Organizing code into horizontal layers like presentation, application, domain, and data, each depending only downward, a common structuring of server applications.

topics.label: Feature vs Layer Structure
topics.desc: The choice between grouping files by technical layer or by feature/domain slice, the latter keeping related code together and scaling better in large apps.

topics.label: Modularity
topics.desc: Decomposing a system into self-contained modules with explicit boundaries and interfaces, so parts can be developed, understood, and replaced independently.

topics.label: Controller-Service-Repository
topics.desc: The common backend separation where controllers handle transport, services hold business logic, and repositories own persistence, keeping each layer thin and testable.

topics.label: Monorepo vs Polyrepo
topics.desc: The repository strategy of one repo holding many projects versus many separate repos, trading atomic cross-project changes and sharing against isolation and simpler ownership.

topics.label: Config & Env Separation
topics.desc: Keeping configuration and secrets out of code and per-environment, via environment variables or config files, so the same build runs in dev, staging, and prod.

topics.label: Monolith
topics.desc: A single deployable unit containing all application logic, simple to build, test, and deploy early on, but prone to tangled coupling and scaling pain as it grows.

topics.label: Modular Monolith
topics.desc: A single deployable with strong internal module boundaries and explicit interfaces, capturing much of microservices' decoupling without distributed-systems overhead.

topics.label: Microservices
topics.desc: An architecture of small, independently deployable services owning their data and communicating over the network, trading operational complexity for team and scaling autonomy.

topics.label: Serverless Architecture
topics.desc: Composing applications from managed, event-triggered functions and services with no servers to provision, billed per use and scaling automatically to zero and back.

topics.label: Backend-for-Frontend
topics.desc: A dedicated backend layer tailored to one frontend or client type, aggregating and reshaping downstream services so each UI gets exactly the API it needs.

topics.label: Event-Driven Architecture
topics.desc: A style where components communicate by emitting and reacting to events rather than direct calls, enabling loose coupling, async workflows, and easy extensibility.

topics.label: Message Queues
topics.desc: Brokers like RabbitMQ, Kafka, or SQS that buffer and route messages between producers and consumers, decoupling services and smoothing load with async processing.

topics.label: API Gateway
topics.desc: A single entry point fronting backend services that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, and aggregation, hiding internal topology from clients.

topics.label: Twelve-Factor App
topics.desc: A methodology of twelve practices, config in the environment, stateless processes, and disposability, for building portable, scalable apps suited to cloud platforms.

topics.label: Vertical & Horizontal Scaling
topics.desc: Handling more load by scaling up to a bigger machine or scaling out across many machines; horizontal scaling underpins most modern web architecture.

topics.label: Load Balancing
topics.desc: Distributing incoming requests across multiple servers via algorithms like round-robin or least-connections, improving throughput, availability, and graceful failover.

topics.label: Caching Layers
topics.desc: Placing fast stores at multiple tiers, browser, CDN, application, and database, to serve hot data quickly and cut load on slower origins behind them.

topics.label: CDNs
topics.desc: Geographically distributed edge servers that cache and serve content near users, reducing latency and origin load for static assets and increasingly dynamic content.

topics.label: Database Scaling
topics.desc: Scaling the data tier through replication, read replicas, sharding, and partitioning, usually the hardest bottleneck since state is far harder to scale than stateless compute.

topics.label: Statelessness
topics.desc: Designing servers to hold no per-client state between requests, pushing session state to a shared store, so any instance can serve any request and scale horizontally.

topics.label: High Availability & Redundancy
topics.desc: Eliminating single points of failure through redundant instances, zones, and failover so the system keeps serving despite component outages and meets uptime targets.

topics.label: Designing for Failure
topics.desc: Assuming components will fail and building in timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation so partial outages do not cascade into total ones.

topics.label: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
topics.desc: Quick capacity math, on traffic, storage, bandwidth, and latency budgets, to sanity-check designs and size resources, a staple skill in system-design interviews.

topics.label: Refactoring
topics.desc: Improving the internal structure of code without changing its external behavior, applied in small safe steps backed by tests to keep the system green throughout.

topics.label: Refactoring Techniques
topics.desc: Concrete moves like extract function, rename, inline, move method, and replace conditional with polymorphism that mechanically transform code toward a cleaner shape.

topics.label: Technical Debt
topics.desc: The implied future cost of expedient shortcuts and aging design, which accrues interest as slower changes and more bugs until deliberately repaid.

topics.label: Identifying & Paying Debt
topics.desc: Surfacing debt through smells, metrics, and pain points, then prioritizing and budgeting cleanup, often alongside features via the boy-scout rule rather than big-bang rewrites.

topics.label: Strangler-Fig Migration
topics.desc: Incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing slices of functionality to new code behind a facade until the old system can be safely retired.

topics.label: Legacy Code
topics.desc: Working safely with inherited, often untested code by characterizing current behavior with tests, finding seams, and changing it gradually without regressions.

topics.label: Code Review
topics.desc: Peer review of changes before merge to catch bugs, enforce standards, and share knowledge, the everyday quality gate practiced through pull requests and constructive feedback.
